documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Gold Capital of Asia

sections.title: A — Gold Capital of Asia
sections.statement:
Chiufen, the old mining town located within the hills in the northeast Taiwan, is a place where you can really experience Taiwan's historical legacy. It was the site of one of the largest gold mines in Asia. Accordingly, Chiufen is often referred to as the Gold Capital of Asia. The compound $\mathrm{KCN}$ is traditionally used to extract gold from ore. Gold dissolves in cyanide ($\mathrm{CN^-}$) solutions in the presence of air to form $\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}$, which is stable in aqueous solution.

$$
4\mathrm{Au(s)}+8\mathrm{CN^-(aq)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}+2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\longrightarrow4\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-(aq)}+4\mathrm{OH^-(aq)}
$$

parts.label: 4.A-1
parts.statement: Draw a structure for $\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}$ showing the spatial arrangements of the atoms.

parts.label: 4.A-2
parts.statement:
How many grams of $\mathrm{KCN}$ are needed to extract $20\ \mathrm{g}$ of gold from ore? Show your work.

Aqua regia, a $3:1$ mixture (by volume) of concentrated hydrochloric acid and nitric acid, was developed by the alchemists as a means to “dissolve” gold. The process is actually a redox reaction with the following simplified chemical equation:

$$
\mathrm{Au(s)}+\mathrm{NO_3^-(aq)}+\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{AuCl_4^-(aq)}+\mathrm{NO_2(g)}
$$

parts.label: 4.A-3
parts.statement: Write down the half reactions, and use them to obtain a balanced redox reaction for this process.

parts.label: 4.A-4
parts.statement:
What are the oxidizing and reducing agents for the 4.A-3 process?

Gold is too noble to react with nitric acid. However, gold does react with aqua regia because the complex ion $\mathrm{AuCl_4^-}$ forms. Consider the following half-reactions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Au^{3+}(aq)}+3\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Au(s)},&E^0&=+1.50\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{AuCl_4^-(aq)}+3\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Au(s)}+4\mathrm{Cl^-},&E^0&=+1.00\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$

An electrochemical cell can be formed from these two redox couples.

parts.label: 4.A-5
parts.statement:
Calculate the formation constant for $\mathrm{AuCl_4^-}$ at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$K=\frac{[\mathrm{AuCl_4^-}]}{[\mathrm{Au^{3+}}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]^4}.$$

parts.label: 4.A-6
parts.statement:
The function of $\mathrm{HCl}$ is to provide $\mathrm{Cl^-}$. What is the purpose of the $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ for the above reaction? Select your answer from the following choices.

- (a) $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is an oxidizing agent.
- (b) $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is a reducing agent.
- (c) $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is a complexing agent.
- (d) $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is a catalyst.

sections.title: B — Gold Nanoparticles
sections.statement: The synthesis and characterization of gold nanoparticles is currently an active research area. The Brust-Schiffrin method for the synthesis of gold nanoparticle ($\mathrm{AuNP}$) allows the facile preparation of thermally stable and air-stable AuNPs of reduced polydispersity with a controlled size distribution ranging in diameter between $1.5$ and $5.2\ \mathrm{nm}$. The preparative procedure is briefly described as follows. An aqueous solution of $\mathrm{HAuCl_4}$ is mixed with a toluene solution of tetra-n-octylammonium bromide. The solution is mixed with dodecanethiol and is treated with an excess of $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$. Formation of the AuNPs is evidenced by the immediate, pronounced darkening of the toluene phase. After ca. $24\ \mathrm{h}$, the toluene solvent is removed with a rotary evaporator and the resulting solid washed on a frit with ethanol and hexane to remove excess thiol. These AuNPs can be repeatedly isolated and re-dissolved in common organic solvents without irreversible aggregation or decomposition.

parts.label: 4.B-1
parts.statement:
Is the methodology for this fabrication referred to a top-down or a bottom-up approach? Select your answer from the following choices.

- (a) Top-down approach, which entails reducing the size of the smallest structures to the nanoscale.
- (b) Bottom-up approach, which involves manipulating individual atoms and molecules into nanostructures.

parts.label: 4.B-2
parts.statement:
The trimethyl-n-octylammonium bromide can also be used as a phase-transfer reagent. It can carry $\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$ from an aqueous phase to an organic phase. Which property does trimethyl-n-octylammonium bromide possess to function as an efficient phase-transfer reagent? Select your answer from the following choices.

- (a) One side of the molecule is electropositive, the other side is electronegative.
- (b) One side of the molecule is hydrophilic, the other side is hydrophobic.
- (c) One side of the molecule is acidic, the other side is basic.

parts.label: 4.B-3
parts.statement:
What is the function of $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ in this preparation? Select your answer from the following choices.

- (a) Reducing agent.
- (b) Oxidizing agent.
- (c) Neutralization agent.
- (d) Complexing agent.

parts.label: 4.B-4
parts.statement:
If the average diameter of a gold nanoparticle is $3\ \mathrm{nm}$, what is the estimated number of Au atoms in each nanoparticle? (The atomic radius of Au is $0.144\ \mathrm{nm}$.) Select your answer from the following choices and show your work.

- (a) $10^2$.
- (b) $10^3$.
- (c) $10^4$.
- (d) $10^5$.

parts.label: 4.B-5
parts.statement:
What is the estimated percentage of Au atoms on the surface of a nanoparticle? Select your answer from the following choices and show your work.

- (a) $20$–$30\%$.
- (b) $40$–$50\%$.
- (c) $60$–$70\%$.
- (d) $80$–$90\%$.

sections.title: 4.A-4
sections.statement: Oxidizing agent: $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ or nitric acid. Reducing agent: Au.

sections.title: 4.A-5
sections.statement:
The printed combination is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Au^{3+}(aq)}+3\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Au(s)},&E^\circ&=1.50\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{Au(s)}+4\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{AuCl_4^-(aq)}+3\mathrm{e^-},&E^\circ&=1.00\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{Au(s)}+\mathrm{Au^{3+}(aq)}+4\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{AuCl_4^-(aq)}+\mathrm{Au(s)},&E^\circ&=+0.50\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The $3\mathrm{e^-}$ terms cancel.

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.059}{n}\log Q.$$

At equilibrium, $Q=K$, $E=0$, and the printed concentration expression is

$$K=\frac{[\mathrm{AuCI_4}]}{[\mathrm{Au^{3+}}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]^4}.$$

$$E=\frac{0.059}{n}\log K,\qquad0.50=\frac{0.059}{3}\log K,\qquad K=10^{25.42}=2.6\times10^{25}.$$

The alternative thermodynamic derivation is

$$\Delta G_1^0+\Delta G_2^0=\Delta G_3^0,$$

$$(-nFE_1^0)+(-nFE_2^0)=-RT\ln K,$$

$$E^\circ=\frac{RT}{nF}\ln K=\frac{0.059}{n}\log K,\qquad0.50=\frac{0.059}{3}\log K,$$

$$K=10^{2542}=2.6\times10^{25}.$$

sections.title: 4.B-4
sections.statement:
Answer: (b). Calculation:

$$V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}=\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^3,\qquad V_{\mathrm{Au}}=\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{Au}}^3,$$

$$N_{\mathrm{Au}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}}{V_{\mathrm{Au}}}=\frac{\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^3}{\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{Au}}^3}=\left(\frac{r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^3}{r_{\mathrm{Au}}^3}\right)^3=\left(\frac{15\ \mathrm{\mathring A}}{1.44\ \mathrm{\mathring A}}\right)^3\approx1000.$$

sections.title: 4B-5
sections.statement:
Method 1:

$$\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^3=\frac43\pi r_{\mathrm{Au}}^3N_{\mathrm{Au}},\qquad r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^3=r_{\mathrm{Au}}^3N_{\mathrm{Au}}.$$

Surface area of a gold nanoparticle:

$$S_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}=4\pi r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}^2=4\pi r_{\mathrm{Au}}^2N_{\mathrm{Au}}^{2/3},$$

$$N_S\approx\frac{S_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}}{\pi r_{\mathrm{Au}}^2}=4N_{\mathrm{Au}}^{2/3},\qquad P\approx\frac{N_S}{N_{\mathrm{Au}}}=\frac4{N_{\mathrm{Au}}^{1/3}}.$$

$N_{\mathrm{Au}}\approx1000$, so $P\approx40\%$.

Or, Method 2:

![](p4-sol-fig2)

$$
P\%=\frac{V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}-V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}'}{V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}}\times100\%
=\frac{V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}/V_{\mathrm{Au}}-V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}'/V_{\mathrm{Au}}}{V_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}/V_{\mathrm{Au}}}\times100\%
=\frac{\left(r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}/r_{\mathrm{Au}}\right)^3-\left(r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}'/r_{\mathrm{Au}}\right)^3}{\left(r_{\mathrm{AuNPs}}'/r_{\mathrm{Au}}\right)^3}\times100\%.
$$

$$P\%=\frac{(15\ \mathrm{\mathring A})^3-(12.12\ \mathrm{\mathring A})^3}{(15\ \mathrm{\mathring A})^3}\times100\%=47\%.$$

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

This attributed 2009 Volume 2 collection prints Part A and Part B as one connected problem. In 4.B-2 it prints $\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$ and trimethyl-n-octylammonium bromide, while the preparative paragraph names tetra-n-octylammonium bromide. These are retained. The key keeps $E^\circ=+1.00\ \mathrm{V}$ next to the reversed oxidation reaction; its equilibrium numerator is typeset “AuCI4” without a visible charge. Its second formation-constant line prints $10^{2542}$, unlike the preceding $10^{25.42}$. The 4.B-4 symbolic radius ratio has an additional outer cube, and the final symbolic denominator in the shell method contains the primed radius, unlike the unprimed numerical denominator. No silent scientific correction is made.

problems.title: Lewis Structure

parts.statement:
Draw one Lewis structure for each of the following molecules.

- a) $\mathrm{N_2}$
- b) $\mathrm{NH_3}$
- c) $\mathrm{O_3}$
- d) $\mathrm{SO_3}$

Draw the Lewis structure of carbon monoxide and assign formal charges and oxidation states to both the carbon and oxygen atoms in carbon monoxide.

Thiourea-S,S-dioxide, $\mathrm{O_2SC(NH_2)_2}$, has the following skeletal structure:

![](p5-fig1)
Draw the Lewis structure of thiourea-S,S-dioxide with zero formal charges on all atoms.
Based on the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) model, what is the geometry around the sulfur, carbon, and nitrogen according to the Lewis structure you predicted from 5.3?

parts.label: 5.4a
parts.statement:
What is the geometry around the sulfur atom? Select your answer from the following choices.

- a) Trigonal pyramidal.
- b) Triangular planar.
- c) T-shape.

parts.label: 5.4b
parts.statement:
Similarly, what is the geometry around the C-atom? Select your answer from the following choices.

- a) Trigonal pyramidal.
- b) Triangular planar.
- c) T-shape.

parts.label: 5.4c
parts.statement:

- a) Trigonal pyramidal.
- b) Triangular planar.

Molecular structure in the solid state is usually determined by X-ray diffraction analysis. According to this method, the structure of thiourea-S,S-dioxide is shown below:

![](p5-fig2)

All the N, H atoms are coplanar with S, C atoms, and the dihedral angle between the OSO plane and the $\mathrm{SC(NH_2)_2}$ plane is $65^\circ$.
Draw the Lewis structure and resonance forms that are consistent with the geometry determined.

problems.title: Alkalinity of Water and Solubility of CO2
problems.statement:
The capacity of water to accept $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions is called alkalinity. Alkalinity is important in water treatment and in the chemistry and biology of natural waters. Generally, the basic species responsible for alkalinity in water are $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$, and $\mathrm{OH^-}$. At pH values below 7, $\mathrm{H^+}$ in water detracts significantly from alkalinity. Therefore, the complete equation for alkalinity in a medium where these are the only contributors can be expressed as

$$\text{alkalinity}=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}].$$

The contributions made by different species to alkalinity depend upon pH. Relevant chemical equations and equilibrium constants at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ are shown below:

| Equilibrium | Constant |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}$ | $K_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=3.44\times10^{-2}$ |
| $\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$ | $K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}=2.00\times10^{-3}$ |
| $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{HCO_3^-}+\mathrm{H^+}$ | $K_{a1}=2.23\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}+\mathrm{H^+}$ | $K_{a2}=4.69\times10^{-11}$ |
| $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}+\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ | $K_{sp}=4.50\times10^{-9}$ |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{H^+}+\mathrm{OH^-}$ | $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ |

**Note: Calculations must be shown.**

parts.statement: Natural waters (river or lake water) generally contain dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$. The ratio of $[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]:[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]:[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]$ in water at $[\mathrm{H^+}]=1.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{M}$ will be $(a):1.00:(b)$. Calculate $(a)$ and $(b)$.

Gaseous $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in the atmosphere can be regarded as a contributor to the alkalinity of water in equilibrium with air. Calculate the concentration of $\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}$ ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) in pure water that is in equilibrium with the unpolluted air at $1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $298\ \mathrm{K}$ containing $0.0360\%$ (molar ratio) $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Assume standard pressure $=1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that the concentration of $\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}$ is equal to $1.11\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{M}$ for further calculations.

The solubility $S$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in water can be defined as

$$S=[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}].$$

The solubility of atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in water that is in equilibrium with the unpolluted air at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ and $1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ will vary with alkalinity.
Find the solubility of atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in pure water ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$). Neglect dissociation of water.

Find the solubility of atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) in a $1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\mathrm{NaOH}$ solution.

At $298\ \mathrm{K}$, $1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ unpolluted air is in equilibrium with natural water saturated with $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$. The following main equilibrium may exist:

$$\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}+\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}+2\mathrm{HCO_3^-}.$$

Calculate the equilibrium constant for the above equation.

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that equilibrium constant $K_{eq}=5.00\times10^{-5}$ for further calculations.

Calculate the concentration of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ($\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$) in $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$-saturated natural water that is in equilibrium with atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that concentration of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}(aq)}=40.1\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$ for further calculations.
Find the alkalinity ($\mathrm{mol/L}$) of the above solution.

In an underground lake saturated with $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, the water has a high content of $\mathrm{CO_2}$. The concentration of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ in this lake was found to be as high as $100\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$. Assume the lake and the air above is a closed system; calculate the effective pressure of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($\mathrm{Pa}$) in air which is in equilibrium with this $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ content.

sections.statement:
$$p(\mathrm{CO_2(aq)})=1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\times3.60\times10^{-4}=36.36\ \mathrm{Pa},$$

$$[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=K_{\mathrm{CO_2}}p(\mathrm{CO_2})=0.0344\times\frac{36.36\ \mathrm{Pa}}{1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}}=1.24\times10^{-5}.$$

If unable to solve, use $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.11\times10^{-5}$ for further calculations.

**(a)**

$$S=[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]\approx[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}].$$

Both $[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]=[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}=2.48\times10^{-8}$ and

$$[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]=\frac{K_{a2}}{[\mathrm{H^+}]/[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}=K_{a2}=4.69\times10^{-11}$$

can be neglected.

$$\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}=K_{a1}K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}=(2.23\times10^{-4})(2.00\times10^{-3})=4.46\times10^{-7}.$$

From 6-2, $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.24\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=2.35\times10^{-6}$.

$$S=1.24\times10^{-5}+2.35\times10^{-6}=1.48\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}.$$

**(b)** Using $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.11\times10^{-5}$:

$$S=[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]\approx[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}].$$

Both $[\mathrm{H_2CO_3}]=[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}=2.22\times10^{-8}$ and $[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]=K_{a2}/([\mathrm{H^+}]/[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}])=K_{a2}=4.69\times10^{-11}$ can be neglected.

$$\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}=K_{a1}K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}=4.46\times10^{-7}.$$

From 6.2, $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.11\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=2.225\times10^{-6}$.

$$S=1.11\times10^{-5}+2.225\times10^{-6}=1.34\times10^{-5}.$$

Using $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.24\times10^{-5}$, the solubility in $1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH is much higher because

$$\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+2\mathrm{OH^-}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}+\mathrm{H_2O},\qquad K=\frac{K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}K_{a1}K_{a2}}{(1.00\times10^{-14})^2}=2.09\times10^{11},$$

$$\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons2\mathrm{HCO_3^-},\qquad K=\frac{K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}K_{a1}}{K_{a2}}=9.37\times10^3.$$

Combining (1) and (2):

$$\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{OH^-}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{HCO_3^-},\qquad K=4.43\times10^7.$$

With such a large $K$ value all $\mathrm{OH^-}$ will finally be converted to $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$.

$$[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=1.00\times10^{-3},\quad[\mathrm{OH^-}]=1.82\times10^{-6},\quad[\mathrm{H^+}]=5.49\times10^{-9},\quad[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]=8.54\times10^{-6}.$$

$$S\approx[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]=1.24\times10^{-5}+1.00\times10^{-3}+8.54\times10^{-6}=1.02\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}.$$

$$K_{eq}=\frac{K_{sp}K_{\mathrm{H_2CO_3}}K_{a1}}{K_{a2}}=\frac{(4.50\times10^{-9})(2.00\times10^{-3})(2.23\times10^{-4})}{4.69\times10^{-11}}=4.28\times10^{-5}.$$

If unable to solve, assume $K_{eq}=5.00\times10^{-5}$ for further calculations.

Each printed branch uses the mass balance $[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=2[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]$ and its specified $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]$ from 6.2.

**(a)** Using $K_{eq}=4.28\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.24\times10^{-5}$, the printed equation is

$$[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=0.510\times10^{-3}=20.5\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}.$$

**(b)** Using $K_{eq}=5.00\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.11\times10^{-5}$:

$$K=5.00\times10^{-5}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}](2[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}])^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]},$$

$$[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=0.5177\times10^{-3}=20.75\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}.$$

**(c)** Using $K_{eq}=5.00\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.24\times10^{-5}$:

$$K=5.00\times10^{-5}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}](2[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}])^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]},$$

$$[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=0.5372\times10^{-3}=21.53\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}.$$

**(d)** Using $K_{eq}=4.28\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=1.11\times10^{-5}$:

$$K=4.28\times10^{-5}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}](2[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}])^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]},$$

$$[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=0.4916\times10^{-3}=19.70\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}.$$

The printed fallback says to assume $[\mathrm{Ca^{2*}}](\mathrm{aq})=40.1$ for further calculations.

$\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ is the major species in solution. Estimate

$$\mathrm{pH}=\frac{\mathrm{p}K_{a1}+\mathrm{p}K_{a2}}2=\frac{3.65+10.33}2=6.99\approx7.00,$$

where $K_{a1}$ and $K_{a2}$ are the dissociation constants of $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$. At pH 7.00, both $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ and $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ can be neglected. Besides, $[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]\ll[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]$ (from 6.1).

problems.title: Kinetic Behaviour of Ozone
problems.statement:
Ozone ($\mathrm{O_3}$) is a form of oxygen. It is a natural component of the stratosphere, where it shields the earth from life-destroying ultraviolet radiation. On absorbing light in this region, ozone is converted to dioxygen molecules.

For the overall reaction of ozone decomposition, $2\mathrm{O_3}\longrightarrow3\mathrm{O_2}$, one of the proposed mechanisms is

$$\mathrm{O_3}\underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}}\mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O_2}\qquad(1),$$

$$\mathrm{O_3}+\mathrm{O}\overset{k_2}{\longrightarrow}2\mathrm{O_2}\qquad(2),$$

where $k_1$, $k_{-1}$, and $k_2$ are the rate constants.

parts.statement: According to the above mechanism what are the differential rate equations for the formation (or consumption) of $\mathrm{O_3}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$, and $\mathrm{O}$ at time $t$, assuming step 2 is irreversible?

Simplification in obtaining the rate law may be found by making appropriate assumptions. Assuming that the concentration of O atoms reaches equilibrium rapidly, its concentration may be given by the equilibrium constant of reaction (1). The second step is rate determining. Under this equilibrium approximation, deduce the differential rate equation for the $\mathrm{O_3}$ depletion as a function of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_3}$ concentrations.

Another assumption frequently made is that the rates of oxygen atom production and consumption are equal (this is called steady state). Under the steady-state approximation, that is $d[\mathrm{O}]/dt=0$, show that the rate equation is

$$-\frac{d[\mathrm{O_3}]}{dt}=\frac{2k_1k_2[\mathrm{O_3}]^2}{k_{-1}[\mathrm{O_2}]+k_2[\mathrm{O_3}]}.$$

One pathway for the destruction of ozone ($2\mathrm{O_3}\longrightarrow3\mathrm{O_2}$) in the upper atmosphere is catalyzed by Freons. For instance, when $\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}$ (Freon-12) migrates to the upper atmosphere, its ultraviolet photolysis may give rise to Cl atoms according to

$$\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}\overset{h\nu}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{CF_2Cl}+\mathrm{Cl}\qquad(3).$$

Chlorine atom can act as a catalyst for the destruction of ozone. The first slow step of a Cl-catalyzed mechanism is proposed as follows:

$$\mathrm{Cl(g)}+\mathrm{O_3(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{ClO(g)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}\qquad(4).$$

Assuming a two-step mechanism, propose the second step in the mechanism.

The activation energy for Cl-catalyzed destruction of ozone is $2.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, while the activation energy for the reaction without the presence of catalyst is $14.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Estimate the ratio of the rate constant for the catalyzed reaction to that for the uncatalyzed reaction at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume the frequency factor is the same for each reaction.

sections.statement:
According to $k=A\exp(-E_a/RT)$, the ratio of rate constants is

$$\text{Ratio}=\exp\left[\frac{(14.0-2.1)\times1000}{8.314\times298}\right]=122.$$

problems.title: Protein Folding
problems.statement:
Most proteins exist usually only in two forms, the native form (N) and the unfolded form (U) when they are thermally or chemically denatured, without appreciable concentrations of other stable intermediates in equilibrium with the native and unfolded forms. For these proteins, the folding-unfolding equilibrium can be described by

$$\mathrm{N}\overset{K(T)}{\rightleftharpoons}\mathrm{U},$$

where N and U denote the folded state (native state) and the unfolded state (denatured state) of the protein, respectively. $K(T)$ is the equilibrium constant for the process at absolute temperature $T$.

parts.statement: What is the equilibrium constant for the process when the native and denatured states are present in equal proportions at equilibrium?
What is the standard free-energy change of the process, $\Delta G^\circ(T)$, when the native and denatured states are present in equal proportions at equilibrium? Express your answer in SI units.

If $(C_N)_{eq}$ and $(C_U)_{eq}$ denote the equilibrium concentrations of N and U in solution, respectively, and $C$ is the total concentration of the protein, the fraction of the total protein that is unfolded under the equilibrium condition is given by $f_U=(C_U)_{eq}/C$. Deduce an expression for $f_U$ in terms of the equilibrium constant $K$. Show all work on the answer sheet.

When a protein is denatured by increasing the temperature of the solution, the fraction of the unfolded protein increases with temperature, as shown in the following figure.

![](p8-fig1)

The midpoint of the denaturation curve is given by $f_U=\frac12$ and $T=T_{1/2}$. The latter is often referred to as the denaturation temperature. At temperatures higher than $T_{1/2}$, $f_U$ increases above $\frac12$, but at temperatures lower than $T_{1/2}$, $f_U$ decreases below $\frac12$.

What is the sign of $\Delta G^\circ(T)$ at temperatures below and above $T_{1/2}$? Select your answer from the following choices.

- a) Negative both below and above $T_{1/2}$.
- b) Positive both below and above $T_{1/2}$.
- c) Positive below $T_{1/2}$, but negative above $T_{1/2}$.
- d) Negative below $T_{1/2}$, but positive above $T_{1/2}$.

How does the standard Gibbs free-energy change for the process vary when the temperature (i) increases above $T_{1/2}$ and (ii) decreases below $T_{1/2}$? Select your answer from the following choices.

- a) Decrease in both cases.
- b) Increase in both cases.
- c) Increases above $T_{1/2}$, but decreases below $T_{1/2}$.
- d) Decreases above $T_{1/2}$, but increases below $T_{1/2}$.

The kinetics of unfolding and refolding of a protein has recently become an intense area of study. We could rewrite the chemical equation as

$$\mathrm{N}\underset{k_b}{\overset{k_f}{\rightleftharpoons}}\mathrm{U},$$

where $k_f$ and $k_b$ denote the forward and backward reaction rate constants, respectively, assuming that both forward and reverse processes are elementary steps that follow first-order kinetics.

For the simple chemical equation and elementary kinetic steps used to describe the protein folding-unfolding process outlined above, what is the relationship between equilibrium constant $K$ and the rate constants $k_f$ and $k_b$?
Derive a rate law for the overall process, that is $dC_U/dt$ in terms of only rate constants, $C_U$ and $(C_U)_{eq}$.

sections.statement: Correct answer: (c). Positive below $T_{1/2}$, but negative above $T_{1/2}$.
Correct answer: (d). Decreases above $T_{1/2}$, but increases below $T_{1/2}$.
